projects.name: MCP Agent Security Gateway
projects.tagline: Security controls for MCP tool calls, agent-to-tool interactions, and AI-agent execution boundaries.
projects.problem: When an AI agent can invoke MCP tools, read files, call APIs, reach databases, or touch cloud and internal services, prompt filtering is no longer the whole security boundary. The risky moment is between the agent deciding to use a tool and that action actually executing.
projects.context: MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets agents call tools. This project places explicit inspection, policy, and observability around that agent-to-tool boundary rather than only inspecting prompts.

actors: An attacker who can influence prompt text, tool metadata, tool arguments, or tool output
surfaces: Tool output returned to the agent

threats.t: Prompt injection carried in tool arguments
threats.mitigation: Argument inspection with Unicode/encoded-payload normalization and injection indicators
threats.residual: Detection is signal-based; novel obfuscation can evade

threats.t: Sensitive-data / PII exfiltration via tool calls or outputs
threats.mitigation: PII and sensitive-data signals, exfiltration indicators, tool-output inspection
threats.residual: No guarantee of catching all encodings

threats.mitigation: MCP server trust and capability checks

threats.residual: Only for traffic observed by the gateway

threats.mitigation: SHA-256 hash-chained audit logging and write-ahead logging
threats.residual: Log storage integrity is the operator's responsibility

architecture.summary: Three runtime surfaces share security components: an inline MCP stdio proxy, a real-time control plane (port 8000), and a separate HTTP inspection service (port 8080). tools/call requests are parsed, normalized, inspected, and allowed or blocked before reaching the downstream server.

implementation: Real inline MCP stdio proxy (python -m mcp_monitor.proxy.stdio_proxy) that sits between client and downstream server
JSON-RPC 2.0 parsing; identifies tools/call; passes through normal protocol messages (initialize, tools/list)
Inline allow/block: a blocking decision returns a JSON-RPC security error and the request is never forwarded
Prompt-injection detection with Unicode and encoded-payload normalization
MCP server trust and capability checks; PII/sensitive-data signals; exfiltration indicators; tool-output inspection
Multi-layer (5-layer) policy evaluation; process-event evaluation; network-egress policy decisions
SHA-256 hash-chained audit logging and write-ahead logging; tracing and metrics
Rate limiting, circuit breakers, and a shadow mode
Docker and Kubernetes deployment templates; adversarial and regression testing
testing: Repository tests cover visible payload behavior
Latency benchmark script (benchmark/tool_call_latency.py) and locustfile present
results: Adoption signal: 17 stars and 5 forks on the public repository (verified on the GitHub profile)
tradeoffs: Inline enforcement adds latency to the tool-call path
Signal-based detection favors coverage of known patterns over guarantees
limitations: Controls only traffic routed through the monitor/proxy; not a substitute for network or kernel-level enforcement
No production-traffic claim; public claims are treated as prototype/security-boundary evidence
The stdio path focuses on JSON-RPC parsing and prompt-injection-oriented tool-argument inspection
lessons: Agent security must move beyond prompt inspection toward action-aware controls at the tool boundary

attack: Prompt-injection and exfiltration indicators are the detection focus

evidence.claim: Inline MCP stdio proxy with inline allow/block
Three runtime surfaces: stdio proxy, control plane :8000, HTTP inspection :8080
SHA-256 hash-chained audit logging
17 stars, 5 forks

evidence.claim: Controls only traffic routed through the monitor/proxy

projects.name: AWS Agent Identity Guard
projects.tagline: Static IAM policy checks for AWS roles used by AI agents and tool executors.
projects.status: Static linter (0.1.0) with STRIDE threat model
projects.problem: AI agents and tool executors can turn over-broad cloud permissions into real actions: invoking Lambda, assuming roles, changing Bedrock/SageMaker control-plane resources, reading secrets, or disabling audit trails.
projects.context: The tool checks IAM policy JSON for agent-specific risk patterns before deployment. It is intentionally narrower than account-wide posture tools and focuses on pre-deploy review of agent roles.

assets: AWS account ID and role/user names
AWS credentials (live mode) — never stored by the tool
actors: An attacker who could supply a crafted policy or tamper with output

threats.mitigation: Parsing via stdlib json.loads; no eval/exec; malformed JSON exits 2
threats.residual: Partial — best-effort linter, not a full IAM semantics engine

threats.mitigation: All actions pinned to commit SHAs; pip-audit in CI
No write IAM APIs; read-only permissions only (iam:List*, iam:Get*, sts:GetCallerIdentity)
max_roles=500 cap; boto3 exponential backoff; ClientError caught

architecture.summary: A CLI reads local IAM policy JSON (or enumerates roles/users read-only in live mode) and runs a deterministic rule engine, emitting text, JSON, or SARIF. Exit code 1 on any high/critical finding lets CI use it as a merge gate.

implementation: 25 deterministic rules across identity policies, trust policies, and permission-boundary presence
Rule IDs AIG001–AIG021 (identity), AIG-TP001–AIG-TP003 (trust policies), AIG-PB001 (permission boundary)
Text, JSON, and SARIF output; SARIF uploads to GitHub Code Scanning for inline PR findings
Zero runtime dependencies for static local-file scanning; optional boto3 live-account scan
Exit code 1 on high/critical findings so a CI workflow can gate merges
controls: AIG002 CRITICAL: wildcard service prefix (bedrock:*, s3:*)
AIG004 CRITICAL: iam:PassRole without iam:PassedToService condition
AIG011 CRITICAL: audit-trail tampering (cloudtrail:StopLogging, GuardDuty, Config)
AIG-TP001 CRITICAL: wildcard principal in trust policy
AIG014 HIGH: S3 write/delete without key-prefix scoping
testing: Deterministic rule tests in tests/ (run isolated with PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1)
pip-audit in CI; GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs
results: Produces reviewable, remediation-oriented findings with exit codes suitable for CI gating
tradeoffs: Intentionally narrow: pre-deploy agent-role review, not account-wide posture
limitations: Static linter: does not call AWS in default mode and does not prove an agent is safe
Not a replacement for IAM Access Analyzer, Prowler, Parliament, CloudTrail, Security Hub, or threat modeling
False negatives are an accepted residual risk; use IAM Access Analyzer for complete analysis
lessons: A small set of deterministic, agent-specific rules with SARIF output can act as a practical pre-deploy gate without cloud access

evidence.claim: 25 deterministic IAM rules with the listed rule IDs
Text, JSON, and SARIF output; SARIF to GitHub Code Scanning
STRIDE threat model; live mode uses read-only IAM APIs only
Static linter, not a replacement for Access Analyzer/Prowler/Parliament
evidence.note: README intro + 'Relationship to Other IAM Tools'

projects.name: HF Model Provenance Scanner
projects.tagline: Scan Hugging Face model repos for provenance, impersonation, pickle-risk, and supply-chain signals.
projects.status: Research scanner with committed regression fixtures
projects.problem: ML model artifacts can become an attack surface before inference: unsafe serialization, repository impersonation, suspicious metadata, and missing provenance signals.
projects.context: The scanner treats model artifacts like software entering a security boundary and emits findings mapped to MITRE ATT&CK v19 for local review or CI.

actors: An attacker who can publish or modify files in a model repository
An impersonator of a trusted organization
boundaries: Untrusted model repository to local/CI review boundary

threats.t: Unsafe deserialization (pickle) leading to code execution
threats.residual: Format support does not imply complete attack coverage

threats.mitigation: Flags missing markers as a risk signal
threats.residual: Missing evidence is a risk signal, not proof of compromise

architecture.summary: The scanner reviews repository files, produces findings with MITRE ATT&CK v19 mappings, and can export an ATT&CK Navigator layer. It integrates as a GitHub Action and a pre-commit hook.

implementation: Format coverage implemented in code: Python, shell/config/dependency files, pickle-derived files, SafeTensors, GGUF, ONNX, and Keras paths
Provenance checks: missing signature, SBOM, and provenance markers can be flagged
Findings mapped to MITRE ATT&CK v19 with 10 HF-specific finding→technique mappings
ATT&CK Navigator layer export (python -m attack_mapping.reporter)
GitHub Action and pre-commit hook integrations
testing: tests/redteam/ contains fixture scripts and reports
results: Fixture suite reports 12 of 12 core incident reproductions detected — fixture evidence only
tradeoffs: Broad format coverage vs. depth of any single format's attack surface
limitations: Fixture pass rates must not be generalized to real-world detection rates
No P99 latency artifact is committed; do not claim latency numbers
No broad clean-model false-positive benchmark; do not claim 0% false positives
Missing evidence is a risk signal, not proof of compromise
lessons: Supply-chain risk is best expressed as reviewable signals with explicit evidence boundaries, not as certainty

evidence.claim: Formats implemented: pickle-derived, SafeTensors, GGUF, ONNX, Keras, plus Python/config/dependency
Findings mapped to MITRE ATT&CK v19; Navigator layer export
evidence.note: README 'MITRE ATT&CK v19 Coverage' and mappings table

evidence.claim: 12/12 core incident fixture reproductions (fixture evidence only)
evidence.note: evidence/DETECTION_PROOF.md; scoped as fixtures in LIMITATIONS.md

projects.name: LLM Red-Team Framework
projects.tagline: Generate adversarial prompts and evaluate an offline detector for LLM red-team experiments.
projects.problem: A detector that performs well on familiar examples may fail against unseen attack styles. The responsible question is not only 'what is the score?' but 'what distribution produced it?'
projects.context: The framework generates adversarial prompts, groups related templates, evaluates an offline detector, and exports SARIF-oriented findings mapped to MITRE ATT&CK v19 and OWASP LLM risks.

actors: An attacker who rephrases, obfuscates, manipulates context boundaries, or escalates across turns

threats.t: Detector memorizes generator templates and overstates generalization
threats.residual: The offline detector remains a first-pass baseline

architecture.summary: Generate prompts → group related templates → evaluate an offline detector → measure → analyze failures, with SARIF export and ATT&CK/OWASP mapping.

implementation: Adversarial prompt generation and template grouping
Offline detector using TF-IDF features with Logistic Regression
Grouped / out-of-distribution evaluation to expose generalization gaps
SARIF-oriented reporting; MITRE ATT&CK v19 and OWASP LLM mappings
testing: Coverage gate configured in the repo
results: Honest operational number: F1 around 0.70 on out-of-distribution transfer evaluation
tradeoffs: A simple TF-IDF/LogReg detector is transparent and fast but is not a semantic defense
limitations: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression are not semantic defenses; this is a research baseline, not a production prompt-injection defense
The project does not test actual LLMs

The README's in-distribution metric table (e.g., higher jailbreak/injection numbers) is tied to eval scripts and is not treated here as an independently reproduced benchmark; the out-of-distribution F1 ~0.70 is the number presented as honest
lessons: Evaluation is part of the security system: without grouped/OOD testing a metric can look better than the detector's real generalization

evidence.claim: Offline TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector with grouped/OOD evaluation
Honest headline: F1 ~0.70 out-of-distribution transfer
evidence.note: Evidence policy: OOD limitation is the number to present, not in-distribution table values

evidence.claim: Does not test actual LLMs; research baseline only

projects.tagline: FGSM / PGD / C&W adversarial robustness benchmark harness — maps to MITRE ATLAS.
projects.problem: Models deployed in adversarial environments (fraud, moderation, biometric auth) can be evaded by small, crafted perturbations.
projects.context: A reproducible adversarial-robustness benchmarking harness that implements classic attacks and produces structured output for security design review. Maps to MITRE ATLAS AML.T0015 (Evade ML Model) and NIST AI RMF MANAGE 2.4.

threats.mitigation: Benchmark runner quantifies vulnerability; CI gate confirms attacks work on a dummy model
threats.residual: Defenses are not implemented in this repo

implementation: FGSM (Goodfellow 2014, L∞), PGD (Madry 2018, iterative L∞), and C&W (Carlini 2017, L2) implemented and unit-tested
Benchmark runner producing structured JSON + CLI output

testing: Attacks are unit-tested for their math properties

Adversarial-training and randomized-smoothing defenses are NOT implemented

Not published on PyPI

projects.name: Dataset Poisoning Detector
projects.tagline: Flag suspicious samples in ML training data — a screening tool, not a silver bullet.
projects.problem: Poisoned training samples can degrade or backdoor a model, but many poisoning attacks leave input features unchanged.
projects.context: A toolkit that runs statistical and density-based anomaly detectors over a feature matrix to surface candidates for human review, wrapped in streaming infrastructure.

actors: An attacker who injects or relabels training samples

threats.t: Label-flip poisoning that does not change features
threats.mitigation: None effective — documented as a fundamental limitation of feature-space detection
threats.residual: High: recommend confident-learning / spectral-signature approaches instead

architecture.summary: Three detectors (z-score, IQR fencing, Isolation Forest) vote in an ensemble; a Kafka/Redis/FastAPI layer explores what a streaming pipeline would look like.

implementation: Three detection methods: z-score, IQR fencing, Isolation Forest
Ensemble majority vote (2 of 3 must agree) to reduce false positives
Kafka / Redis / FastAPI streaming infrastructure around the detector
results: ROC-AUC ~0.53–0.56 on a CIFAR-10 label-flip benchmark — only modestly above random chance
tradeoffs: Well-engineered streaming pipeline wrapping an algorithm that needs fundamental replacement
limitations: ROC-AUC ~0.53–0.56 on CIFAR-10 label-flip: near random; positioned as a research baseline, not production detection
Feature-space anomaly detection cannot catch label-flip attacks that don't change features
About 5% actual false-positive rate at a 5% target; any 'zero false positives' claim would be a reporting error
For production use, prefer confident-learning (CleanLab) or spectral signatures
lessons: Sound infrastructure cannot rescue a detection approach that is blind to the attack class it faces

evidence.claim: ROC-AUC ~0.53–0.56 on CIFAR-10 label-flip (near random)
Cannot catch feature-preserving label-flip attacks; ~5% FPR

philosophy.principle: Secure the action, not just the prompt.
philosophy.detail: The dangerous moment in an agentic system is the handoff from a generated decision to an executed action. Controls belong at that boundary.

philosophy.principle: A metric is meaningful only with its scope attached.
philosophy.detail: In-distribution scores, dummy models, and fixtures each have limits. State the distribution and the model before stating the number.

philosophy.principle: A documented weakness beats an undocumented promise.
philosophy.detail: Every project names what it does not do. Archiving PulseNet was the honest outcome of that discipline.

philosophy.principle: Least privilege is a pre-deploy decision.
philosophy.detail: Over-broad IAM permissions become real actions once an agent holds them; catch them before they ship.

faq.q: What do you do / what is your focus?
faq.a: I build security controls for the moment AI stops generating text and starts taking actions — inspecting agent tool calls, constraining cloud identity for agent workloads, and checking model artifacts before they are trusted.

faq.q: What is your strongest or most notable project?
faq.a: MCP Agent Security Gateway is the flagship: it inspects and gates MCP tool calls at the agent-to-tool boundary and is the most-adopted repo (17 stars, 5 forks). AWS Agent Identity Guard is the strongest IAM piece: a 25-rule static linter with SARIF output and a STRIDE threat model.

faq.q: How do you handle prompt injection?
faq.a: Two ways. In MCP Agent Security Gateway I inspect tool-call arguments with Unicode/encoded-payload normalization and injection indicators, and can block before forwarding. In LLM Red-Team Framework I evaluate a detector with grouped/out-of-distribution splits so its generalization isn't overstated.

faq.q: What is your IAM / least-privilege work?
faq.a: AWS Agent Identity Guard is a static IAM linter with 25 deterministic rules for agent roles — wildcard prefixes, iam:PassRole without conditions, audit-tampering, credential-harvest chains — with text/JSON/SARIF output and a CI merge gate. It runs with no AWS credentials by default.

HF Model Provenance Scanner treats model files as software crossing a trust boundary: it checks pickle-derived, SafeTensors, GGUF, ONNX, and Keras files plus provenance markers, and maps findings to MITRE ATT&CK v19. Its strongest evidence is a 12/12 core-incident fixture suite — labeled as fixture evidence, not a real-world detection rate.

faq.q: Can I see the evidence / prove it?
faq.a: Yes. Every substantive claim on this site links to its source repository, file, or section. Use the 'Prove it' action on any answer, or open a project to see problem, threat model, controls, testing, results, and limitations with links.

faq.q: What are you exploring or currently learning?
faq.a: The through-line I'm extending is action-aware AI security: connecting the agent tool boundary (MCP gateway) with cloud identity constraints (IAM guard) and detection mappings to MITRE ATT&CK / ATLAS. I present these as active engineering, not finished products.

faq.q: What is your experience and education?
faq.a: Cybersecurity Innovation Researcher in ASU's TEM 598 Technology Innovation Lab (with Honeywell Aerospace Innovation Hub), and a Graduate Teaching Assistant / IT Grader at Arizona State University. Two peer-reviewed publications (IEEE 2024, IOSR-JCE 2023). Location: Greater Phoenix Area, AZ.

faq.q: Are you available for work / what roles?
faq.a: Open to AI Security Engineer, ML Security Engineer, and Applied AI/ML Security roles. Based in the Greater Phoenix Area, AZ; F-1 OPT.

faq.q: Are these production systems with customers?
faq.a: No — and the site never claims that. These are research and prototype security tools with explicit limitations. MCP Agent Security Gateway controls only traffic routed through it; the HF scanner's numbers are fixture-scoped; the dataset-poisoning detector is near random on its benchmark and is labeled a research baseline.
